paras: The shooting of Police Chief Hayes and threatened lynching at Crookston, Minnesota, followed an attack on the night of October 19, 1888, in which a man described as a tramp fired six shots at Hayes from behind. The shooter was arrested at once, and newspapers reported 'strong talk of lynching' him, but no attack on the jail was reported, and in December he was convicted in court.
According to the wire story, the man said he shot Hayes because the chief had arrested him for drunkenness the day before, a Thursday.

Hayes was talking with a group of friends that night when the man came up behind him, drew a revolver and fired six times. One bullet struck Hayes in the arm and two entered his left side, and the first reports called him fatally wounded. The shooter was 'promptly arrested', and the shooting caused 'intense excitement' in the town.

Talk of lynching followed, and the St. Paul Daily Globe's headline said an 'excited populace' threatened to hang him. A later Minnesota rewrite added that the sheriff 'had taken extra precautions to prevent the mob from stringing up the prisoner', who was held in the county jail. None of the coverage describes a crowd gathering at the jail or any attempt to seize him.

At the December term of court in Crookston, James Payton, 'the man who shot Chief of Police Hayes', was convicted of assault with intent to kill and returned to jail to await sentence. Placed back in his cell, Payton tried to beat his head against the bars and, after being tied to the floor, tore the flesh from both arms with his teeth, according to the Globe. No report of his sentence, or of Hayes's death or recovery, appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers mainly through one dispatch, which the St. Paul Daily Globe ran as a special dated October 19 and which papers in Washington, New York, Indianapolis and Annapolis reprinted over the next three days. Headlines treated Hayes as dead before any death was reported: 'Killed for Doing His Duty' in the Washington Evening Star, 'A Police Captain Killed by a Tramp' in the New York Sun, and 'Murdered Out of Revenge' in the Annapolis Evening Capital. The Annapolis version left out the lynching talk entirely, as did a one-line item in the Morris Tribune.
The Globe's December follow-up, headed 'Cannibalistic Payton', dwelt on the prisoner's self-injury rather than his trial. No paper named the race of either man.

The October reports called Hayes fatally wounded and his shooter a 'murderer', but the December conviction was for assault with intent to kill, a charge that does not suggest Hayes died. The wire also called Hayes both 'Captain of Police' and 'Chief', while the Minnesota papers consistently called him chief.

accounts.label: Wire report (Crookston special)
accounts.gist: A tramp fired six shots at Hayes from behind, fatally wounding him, was promptly arrested, and gave as his reason that Hayes had arrested him for drunkenness; the shooting caused 'intense excitement' and talk of lynching.

accounts.label: Mower County Transcript rewrite
accounts.gist: Repeats the wire and adds that the sheriff took extra precautions to keep the mob from hanging the prisoner in the county jail.

accounts.label: Crookston court report
accounts.gist: In December James Payton was convicted of assault with intent to kill for shooting Hayes and then badly injured himself in his cell.

framing.detail: The St. Paul Globe's headline said an 'Excited Populace Threatens to Hemp the Muderer Into Eternity', calling the shooter a murderer while Hayes was still described as wounded.
Eastern and midwestern papers ran the wire under headlines casting Hayes as killed on duty ('Killed for Doing His Duty', 'Murdered Out of Revenge').
The December Globe item headed 'Cannibalistic Payton' focused on the prisoner's self-injury in his cell.

Object of the lynching threat: the arrested 'tramp', named in December as James Payton; race not stated. Shooting victim: Chief (or Captain) of Police Hayes.
Accused of shooting Chief of Police Hayes six times from behind; later convicted of assault with intent to kill
